column17: The Moose Creek Bowl tops out just below the summit around 14,100'. The top 300' of the bowl are the steepest ranging between 25-40 degrees. This starting zone is about 900' wide and 300' tall. The bowl shape ranging in aspect from SE -> NE acts as a terrain trap, funneling snow into the constricted gully below. The runout of the path then crosses a mining road at about 13,570'. The runout then continues down the Moose Creek Gully at a 20-30 degree angle down to 13,200' where the pitch steepens lower in the gully.
column18:
Leading up to the day of the avalanche, our party had discussed options for skiing, and decided to ski the Moose Creek Bowl of Mt Bross based on a video from the week prior which showed exceptional coverage for October. With the week of warm and wet weather before, we discussed that the snow underneath would likely be a firm melt freeze crust. On Saturday, it was forecasted to snow 5-10cm of snow on Mt Bross with moderate winds. We discussed that the new wind drifted snow overlying the firm crust would provide for possibly good skiing, but avalanche hazard was not discussed. Upon arrival to the trailhead on Sunday morning, we found ~10cm of new snow, and we were stoked about the prospect of good skiing. We also observed multiple other groups who had the same idea and were headed in the direction of Moose Creek Bowl. We quickly skinned up the Dolly Varden road before traversing to look at Moose Creek Bowl. It had great coverage, but we noticed the top 100 feet of the bowl looked smooth and pillowed, with wind drifted snow that looked like it might host a small but reactive wind slab. We discussed the possibility of an avalanche and agreed that it would most likely be isolated, and probably D1 in size; something relatively harmless to a skier. We continued up the east ridge, setting a skin track with two other groups of two closely behind. The spatial variability was large here, and surface conditions ranged from pencil hard old snow, to a dense wind drifted slab up to 20 cm thick. We noticed moderate cracking and collapsing, and figured there was probably some weak snow resting on the rocks below that caused those places with deeper wind drifted snow to collapse. Skier 3 dug a quick hand pit, and found the wind drifted snow to shear on the crust below, but we determined that this slab was isolated and unlikely to propagate across the entire slope. As we continued up the ridge, we watched a party of 3 ski the lookers right side of the bowl. The top looked like firm wind drifted snow but it looked to quickly soften into good powder 100' down. We were stoked. 
As we reached the top of the bowl, we hurried our transition with the intention of skiing the bowl before the other groups behind us. We decided on skiing the center of the bowl. Skiers 2 and 3 both felt nervous about skiing this slope, but didn't say anything because the snow cover is so thin, an avalanche seemed unlikely, and the rest of the group seemed stoked. Skier 1 felt that there was potential for a slide as well, but thought that it would be a small isolated wind slab, D1 in size that would easily be managed on skis.
Skier 3 suggested that Skier 1 perform a ski cut to mitigate the hazard safely, but Skier 1 didn't want to do that and communicated that they were going to ski it fast down the center.
The group completed a beacon check before leaving the top, and Skier 1 promptly skied down the slope, noticing no signs of instability and stopping on the mining road in the center of the path 500 feet down. Skier 1 noticed that the wind drifted snow near the top of the starting zone was supportable to skis and hollow sounding, but quickly transitioned to softer, shallower new snow. Skier 1 did not communicate this to Skiers 2 and 3.
After a brief pause, Skier 2 dropped. 3 turns and about 40 feet down, a slab collapsed and propagated about 370 feet wide, and 100 feet vertically. Initially, the slab propagated only on the old/new snow interface with the wind drifted snow, but then quickly stepped down to the ground on a likely persistent grain type.
Skier 2 yelled, and was quickly swept off their feet and began to get carried down the slope. Skier 1 noticed the avalanche was gaining momentum, and skied down and skiers right to avoid being hit by the avalanche. Skier 3 lost sight of Skier 2 in the avalanche about 200 feet down, but visualized that Skier 1 was not caught. Skier 2 was tumbled in the avalanche and lost their right ski somewhere in the slide when the leash broke. Skier 2 came to a stop with their head above the snow and their left ski attached with the leash, anchoring their foot. A second later, another wave of snow hit Skier 2 from behind and fully buried them in the snow face down, because the leash had anchored their foot and buried their head downhill.
 As the debris stopped and Skier 2 was not visible, Skier 3 began a beacon search for the one buried person. Skier 1 also began searching from the bottom up, bootpacking up the debris. After about 3 minutes, Skier 1 got a signal at 45 m and Skier 3 almost at the same time got a signal of 30 m. Skier 3 rapidly skied to within 5 meters of the burial before noticing a hole in the debris, where Skier 2's backpack was just barely visible. Skier 3 yelled to Skier 1, deployed their shovel and began excavating Skier 2. At just under 5 minutes after the avalanche, Skier 3 uncovered Skier 2's airway and did a finger sweep to clear the snow from their airway, and reported that Skier 2 wasn't breathing. Skier 1 arrived to help. Skier 2 began snoring respirations but was still unresponsive. Skiers 1 and 3 continued to dig out the rest of Skier 2, and kept an open airway. Skier 2 resumed regular respirations, and became responsive as they were getting rolled onto their back. Skier 2 was given layers, and after assessment no injuries were found. 
Nearby parties had initiated 911, but after the decision was made to self-rescue, SAR and additional resources was called off.
The positive outcome of this incident was very lucky, and had the rescue time been much slower, things could have ended much differently.
All 3 skiers were equipped with beacon, shovel, and probe but none of the skiers were wearing an airbag.

Skier-triggered avalanche on far skier left of Y Chute (slope 35-40 degrees), where there are some rocks, a more convex shape and less relative shade. At 9:30am, we were deciding to go back up to Current Creek Bench or ski Hidden Knoll back to the parking lot. It felt much warmer than the forecast and seemed above freezing. We saw roller balls on east-facing slopes underneath cornices on Current Creek bench, so we decided to head back down to the lot instead of opting for a longer last run from the top of the bench. Based on the forecast (danger level 1 near treeline) and our experience on the snow that day, we thought the steeper angle terrain in the chute would be stable. I went first down the middle and skier right of the chute, which was tracked by maybe 5 previous people since the last snowfall. Very minor sloughing from turns. My friend then went skier left, which was untracked and above some rocks (see photo). After his second turn, he triggered a wet-loose avalanche roughly 15-20 feet wide and was able to ski out of it quickly to the side of the chute. The slide funneled in the rocks and slid another 30-40 feet down the chute.

The snowboarder was able to cut out of the avalanche and was not caught. The debris dissipated when it reached the open lower angle run out zone.   The crown was approximately 9-12 inches at the deepest point, only the most recent snow was entrained in the avalanche .  It ran for estimated 450 vertical feet. The third rider descended the easterly aspect with out incident.  \nSome spindrifts were observed earlier in the day when the winds were higher. Some small point releases, that seemed to have occurred during the storm, were observed during the approach of the first run.  The first run was on a similar aspect and slightly lower elevation, it produced some sluffs but no major instabilities were observed on the first run or either approach .

Small loose dry avalanches were reactive to ski pressure on slopes steeper than about 35 degrees, These avalanches were slow-moving and steeper slopes over 38 degrees were needed to get them moving more than a few feet.\n\nI also saw old wet slab avalanche debris for a large D2 avalanche. This is notable because I traveled in this area on the 24th and did not see this slide. This large avalanche failed naturally sometime between the morning of the 24th and the 29th, which is over a week into the warming trend and days after humans triggered similar avalanches on adjacent slopes. This is just another observation that highlights the tricky nature of wet slab avalanches and periods of extended warming.

This avalanche is one of a trend of avalanches Highlands Snow safety team seem to be intentionally triggering during the first major warm up of the spring. They placed some explosives last week (need to put this observation in still) and only got relatively small results, not what they were hoping for. I will double check but Highlands bowl has been closed for multiple days with no overnight freezes before they triggered this avalanche. This was the first one coded as a Wet Slab of this trend of large wet avalanches they intentionally trigger in the spring that I know of in the last 5 years. They reported using a 116-pound ANFO shot on the snow surface to trigger this one.

Skied from the summit of Whetstone, mostly skiing east and southeast aspects. Up top, the snow was either punchy wind crusts or barely edgable sun crust. The snow began to get slightly softer at around 11,000 feet. We then skied through some tight trees and found ourselves on top of a thin SE-facing aspect that we had walked up earlier in the day, barely breaking the snow surface. We then noticed the temperature starkly increase and our skis sinking deep into the snow. The first skier in our party got about halfway down the first ~100 foot pitch, which slid behind him. He was able to ski out of the slide path, staying on his feet and avoiding the avalanche altogether. After the snow settled, a second member of our party skied along the top of the ridge above the first slide and triggered a second, smaller avalanche. This was a wet slab with a ~20 cm crown that slid on a snow surface just above ground level. The crown was about 50 feet wide, and the avalanche was about 100 ft long.

column19: I first observed these avalanches on Sunday 3/1. They looked fresh with only the 1” of new snow (from 3/1) over the debris, so guessing they occurred around 2/27 to 2/28. Multiple heavily wind loaded rollovers released above the standard Sangree Hut approach trail at the horse-shoe curve. There was a surprisingly large amount of snow involved in the largest slide.  Width was 800-1000’ wide with blocks 2-3 feet thick. Some adjacent slopes on the same aspect that did not slide were bare dirt. It looked like these slides were a combination of natural cornices and wind pillows failing on facets and sliding at least partially over pre-existing bare ground. \n\nPhotos were taken between 3/1 and 3/4, some after it warmed up and melted the debris a bit.

Saw and photographed this avalanche on 3/4, but estimated it occurred on 2/28 based on the amount of new snow covering the debris. Guessing it slid on facets based on other slides in the area. \n\nThe photo of the South side of Buckeye Peak shows a larger, older avalanche likely triggered from a natural cornice fall.

The first open slope over 30 degrees that I encountered today was remotely triggered as I approached it from about 10 feet away. This avalanche, on a relatively small slope, then ran over the bench below it into steeper terrain lower down and sympathetically triggered numerous other avalanches that ran hundreds of feet snapping branches and small vegetation.
A few hundred feet higher while walking along the ridge I got a big collapse that I didn't realize triggered an avalanche until I heard branches snapping a few seconds later hundreds of feet below me. This avalanche sympathetically triggered another D2 around 1000 feet from where I initially got the collapse.
Near the summit of Green Mountain I got a rumbling collapse on the west side of the ridgeline and watched cracks travel hundreds of feet across low-angle terrain in front of me, then about 8 seconds later on the east-side of the ridgeline I noticed a rumbling collapse traveling back towards me shaking full grown trees, travel past me, then a few seconds later the collapse came back up behind me along the west-side of the ridgeline again. As I walked up and over the next knoll, I realized this triggered an avalanche with a crown face over 8 feet tall. The total height of snow where I initially triggered the collapse was 46cm.
Walking further along the ridgeline, I remotely triggered another avalanche about as big as the slope could go and grew large enough to snap a few trees about 4 inches in diameter.
I have no doubt that I triggered numerous other avalanches on slopes that were too far away for me to clearly see crowns, especially on the west side of the ridgeline.

I also observed several older avalanches that likely ran during the storm as well as a few recent avalanches that likely ran in the last 24 hours.

Caribou Basin is a high-elevation drainage that runs east to west. It is located between Snake Creek and Lavina Creek, west of Midway, UT. The narrow basin has short, steep, north-facing slopes that are prone to frequent avalanching during the winter months. The avalanche occurred on a northeast-facing slope at 9600 feet. The starting zone is a predominantly planar 36-degree slope with a distinct, very steep convexity mid-slope where the slope angle increases to more than 40 degrees. Looking down the slope, the left side has a band of old-growth trees, and the right side has a near-vertical rock band with a 15-25-foot-tall cliff. The runout is free of vegetation but has a notable bench and terrain feature on the looker's left side below the trees that deflects debris to the right into low-angle terrain. On the south-facing side of the ridge is a low-angle slope with sparse trees and sagebrush. This creates a high-volume fetch area of snow for wind to transport and deposit on the leeward side of the ridge.
This area is categorized as ‘Challenging’ using the Avalanche Terrain Exposure Scale. Challenging terrain is defined by ‘exposure to well-defined avalanche paths, starting zones, terrain traps, or overhead hazard. Options exist to reduce or eliminate exposure with careful routefinding.’
The avalanche occurred on a northeast-facing slope at 9640 feet. The crown measured 2-3 feet thick and more than 475 feet wide. The slab consisted of several hard layers of recent storm snow and wind-drifted snow from the mid-February storm cycle. The avalanche failed on a layer of depth hoar that developed during a prolonged period of clear weather in January. The bed surface was a slick ice crust that formed during a widespread rain-on-snow event on December 24. The avalanche danger for that area was rated CONSIDERABLE that day, with a Special Avalanche Bulletin warning that “With improving weather moving in for the weekend, avalanche accidents are likely in the backcountry.”

The avalanche occurred on a north-facing slope in Butler Basin in Big Cottonwood Canyon within the Uinta Wasatch Cache National Forest. The slope was a 38-degree sub ridge leading toward Gobblers Knob and held large trees.

The crown was located at approximately 9,300 feet in elevation. The avalanche was approximately 275 feet wide and one to two feet deep. It ran roughly 100 vertical feet before abruptly stopping on a flat bench at approximately 9,200 feet.

The crown was located at 9,300 feet on a north/northwest aspect directly off a subridge. At the crown profile location, the slope angle measured 36 degrees, consistent with the surrounding slope, which averaged 38 degrees. Crown depths averaged one to two feet. The slab consisted of F to 1F-hard precipitation and wind-broken particles within the upper 42 cm of the snowpack. From 122 to 93 cms, the snowpack was composed of very hard 2 mm precipitation particles from the February 16 to 19 storm. Between 93 and 80 cm, the snow consisted of 2 mm wind-broken particles.

The slab rested on an F-minus hardness layer of weak faceted snow, with grains 1 to 2 mm in size. This initial faceted layer, from 80 to 69 cm, overlaid a slightly harder 4F layer of larger 2 to 3 mm facets. The decomposing Christmas Eve rain crust was present between 46 and 40 cm, with 2-3 mm moist facets extending to the ground below the crust.

The primary failure plane appeared to be within the F-minus faceted layer between 80 and 69 cm, though in some areas the avalanche stepped down into the deeper faceted layer between 69 and 46 cm.

The terrain was unforgiving, with the steep slope ending abruptly in a flat area at the bottom, where the debris accumulated deeply.

From 2.19 Ob: Very chilly, mostly sunny day today with light winds. Explosives mitigation produced results but not as many as could be expected after such a loading event. Snow was most sensitive in heavily wind-loaded areas on north aspects near and mostly above tree line. Surprisingly little natural activity was evident in the ski area or the surrounding backcountry. There were a few small storm slab avalanches in Alta Lakes and it appeared that the NE Bowl of Lizard Head produced a large avalanche at some point yesterday. Notable explosives triggered avalanches in the ski area include:

 

Bald 5 “Super Chub” (N, 11,400’ AE SS D1.5 O 2-3’ crown face)

GH 1 “Top Rocks” (NW, 12,400’ AE HS D2 O) with a five foot crown face and running over the cliff.

GH1 “Feeder Face” also ran over the cliff (NW, 12,300’ AE HS D2 I 4-6’ crown face)

GH1 “ET’s” (NW, 12k AE SS D1 I)

Easy Chute (N, 11,900’ AA SS D2 S) stepped down into old snow HS in lower Nice Chute).


Lack of naturals in the local zone and ski area and relatively few explosives results are pointing to a considerable rather than high hazard in our area of the San Juan’s. A forecasted 4-8” of snow tonight into tomorrow with ideal moderate S/SW loading winds will keep the hazard elevated and give us another early morning. Rest up!

Remotely triggered 2 large avalanches on an east and a northeast aspect. 

The avalanche on a NE aspect propagated widely across the terrain and produced a large, deep debris pile. 

The Easterly facing avalanche was remotely triggered while skiing a nearby connected slope. Notably, we had jumped on the side of the slope and produced a couple of collapses. After giving up on the remote trigger, we went skiing on a smaller slope in the area, and the 2nd skier got a collapse that triggered this avalanche remotely.

column19: We attempted to remotely trigger this avalanche to gauge sensitivity. The first heavy jump above the slope produced a collopse that shook snow out of trees but didn't produce an avalanche. A large jump from another location above the slope triggered the avalanche. This crown was around 700ft wide, measured as a straight line across the terrain. The avalanche ran surprisingly far into the forest below, breaking some ~4" diameter trees. Wide sections of the debris pile were 150cm deep. The crown averaged 70cm as a best guess.
